title: 'What Do You Need?' Wednesday: Spooky Season
author: Episcopal Academy CTL
summary: This weekly teaching digest from the Episcopal Academy Center for Teaching and Learning uses Halloween as a frame for four research-based items, each paired with a classroom move. It first revisits the learning styles myth, citing a Hattie and O'Leary review of 17 meta-analyses with an effect size of d = .04 against the fact that 89 percent of educators still believe in it. It then describes a 2017 study in which young children persevered longest when they checked in on themselves as a pretend character such as Batman. The third item recommends pretesting, giving a quiz on material not yet taught and returning it at the end of the lesson, while noting the benefit is limited to the tested material. The closing item recounts Diener's 1976 trick-or-treat experiment, which suggests that being known by name makes integrity easier. Linked studies were not expanded into separate records.
points: Matching instruction to a preferred learning style has an effect size near zero, so choose the mode that fits the content and use it with everyone.
Having young children ask whether a pretend hero is still working hard measurably lengthened their persistence on a dull task.
Pretesting works best when the questions target the main ideas, and the same questions can be returned at the end of class as a self-check.
Diener's trick-or-treat study suggests anonymity increases misbehaviour, which makes knowing each student by name a practical integrity strategy.
quotes: When studies actually test the idea of matching instruction to a student’s preferred style, the effect size is d = .04, which is, statistically speaking, very little. And yet a 2020 review of 37 surveys found that 89% of educators still believe in them.
Learners might have a preference, but the evidence that matching the medium to that preference leads to more learning is thin. Pick the mode that fits the material and use it with everyone.
For both ages, the pretend character intervention saw the highest percentage of time on task, followed by the third-person method, and then the traditional method.
The answer, it seems, is that guessing first and then learning the right answer tends to stick better than just learning it.
Open your next lesson with three “trick” questions on the main ideas. Let students guess, hold off on the answers, and teach.
Learners routinely fail to realize how well it works (Mera et al., 2025)—so expect a few (non-zombie related) groans.

Children who arrived in groups and stayed anonymous behind their costumes took extra 57% of the time, while children who came alone and had been asked their names and addresses did so just 7.5% of the time.
doing the right thing comes easier when you’re known—which is one more reason the work we do to know each student by name (and by far more than name) matters.
